extracted.intended_audience: EPA policymakers, agency scientists, and legal counsel preparing regulatory comments
extracted.subtask_description: A technical-legal comment on a proposed repeal or revision of an EPA endangerment finding, evaluating the scientific adequacy of the agency's supporting report (Draft CWG Report) across topics such as sea level rise, climate models, attribution, CO2 fertilization, and ocean change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple datasets and lines of evidence for sea level rise
rubrics_metrics.description: An understanding of sea level rise and projections is necessarily based on multiple datasets; satellite altimetry and observations of land ice changes and ocean heat corroborate global mean sea level rise and acceleration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a single type of measurement. Combine tide gauges, satellite altimetry, land-ice mass balance, ocean heat content, and paleo sea-level records to evaluate trends and acceleration. Cite paleo evidence (e.g., Pliocene sea levels) and modern datasets together to form robust conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for local processes and variability when interpreting tide-gauge data
rubrics_metrics.description: Local effects on sea level rise due to ocean circulation, glacial isostatic rebound, and local land compaction are well known and discussed in the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing regional or site-specific sea-level trends, explicitly account for uplift/subsidence, local ocean dynamics, and other local processes. Do not equate lower rates at some sites (e.g., U.S. West Coast) with absence of global or regional acceleration without mechanistic explanation (e.g., Cascadia uplift, GIA, multidecadal variability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cherry-picking and selective site choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Draft CWG Report selects a small subset of data to fit its predetermined conclusions (e.g., picks five sites out of many and draws broad conclusions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not draw scientific conclusions from a non-representative subset of sites or data without justification. Provide statistical context and rationale for site selection; perform analyses on the full, representative dataset or demonstrate that selected sites are unbiased and statistically meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require statistical analysis and significance testing for trend/acceleration claims
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to make a scientifically sound conclusion based on specific sites taken out of a statistically meaningful context and without analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support claims about acceleration or lack thereof with appropriate statistical tests, trend analyses, and measures of uncertainty. Present significance levels, confidence intervals, and rationale for time windows chosen. Avoid relying on visual inspection or anecdotal site examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate climate models across ensembles and consider observational uncertainties
rubrics_metrics.description: Model results undergo rigorous study—both within a particular model and across groups of independently developed models—and are compared with observations where possible; discrepancies (e.g., CMIP6 tropospheric warming vs some observational products) are explained by observational uncertainties, internal variability, and uncertain historical forcings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess model performance using multi-model ensembles, consider ensemble means vs individual realizations, and explicitly account for observational dataset versions, homogenization issues, diurnal-cycle corrections, and stratospheric contamination. Do not treat model–observation differences as automatic refutation of anthropogenic attribution without investigating these causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overinterpret model limitations as refutation of anthropogenic attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to implications in the Draft CWG Report, CMIP6 model outputs do not diminish scientific confidence in the influence of human activity in driving climate change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between model uncertainty and the multiple independent lines of evidence (fingerprinting, energy-budget constraints, paleoclimate) that support anthropogenic attribution. Use model advances as tools for understanding complexity rather than reasons to discard attribution conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple independent lines of evidence for attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribution of climate change is supported by the physical understanding of the climate system and multiple lines of evidence (e.g., fingerprinting including stratospheric cooling, ocean heat uptake, paleoclimate and energy-budget constraints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing observed warming (or impacts) to greenhouse gases, combine physical theory, fingerprinting studies, observed vertical and spatial patterns (e.g., stratospheric cooling), ocean heat uptake, and paleoclimate context rather than relying on a single method or dataset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctly interpret and apply event-attribution science
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate change attribution can assess whether and to what extent individual extreme events’ impacts are attributable to climate change; climate change exacerbates frequency and severity rather than acting as a binary sole cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the logical fallacy that an event must be either caused by climate change or not. Use rapid attribution (e.g., World Weather Attribution) and subsequent peer-reviewed studies; recognize that attribution often quantifies changes in likelihood or intensity (e.g., heatwaves made X°F hotter, rainfall Y% heavier).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat climate sensitivity evidence in context and avoid selective citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevailing estimates of climate sensitivity—including those cited by the report—reinforce the necessity of urgent and sustained reductions; cherry-picking studies to suggest lower sensitivity is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on comprehensive assessments (e.g., IPCC) that synthesize multiple methods and datasets. If citing outlier studies, explain why they differ and whether their methods have been critiqued or remain subject to debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for internal (natural) variability without conflating it with long-term trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal variabilities (PDO, AMO, ENSO) affect short-term variations but do not change the net energy of the Earth system and thus do not explain long-term warming trends; assessments of trends account for these patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate short-term, regionally varying signals due to internal variability from long-term anthropogenic trends. Use methods that separate internal variability from forced responses when evaluating trends and model–data comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider limitations and negative impacts of CO2 fertilization (greening)
rubrics_metrics.description: CO2 fertilization effects are limited by water and nutrient constraints, may slow over time, and can produce negative outcomes (spread of nuisance plants, increased allergens, decreased nutritional value); greening does not offset warming harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating increased greenness as an unequivocal benefit. Evaluate CO2 fertilization in the context of vapor pressure deficit, nutrient limitations, water demand, differential species responses, ecosystem function (not just greenness), and impacts on human health and food nutrition. Cite literature showing slowing greening trends and limits of fertilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-CO2 feedbacks and cascading feedback processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The chapter does not address CO2 feedbacks that can drive additional warming through other gases (e.g., methane from wetlands), ice loss, permafrost thaw, and soil carbon emissions; many models may not include these feedbacks which generally result in further warming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing net impacts of increased CO2, account for feedback loops (permafrost carbon release, methane, ice-albedo, etc.) and either include them in modeling or discuss their likely direction and magnitude. Recognize that including only CO2 fertilization without feedbacks can misrepresent net effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate ocean impacts holistically (warming, stratification, deoxygenation, acidification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed impacts of CO2 on the oceans are largely related to ocean warming including heatwaves, stratification, deoxygenation, and declining surface pH; focusing solely on ocean acidification ignores major drivers and combined effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ocean change by considering multiple stressors together (temperature, chemistry, oxygen), their interactions, and impacts on ecosystems (e.g., coral bleaching). Historic mass extinctions implicate combined changes in pH, temperature, and oxygenation; future risk depends on combined drivers and emissions trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not minimize harmful overall impacts by focusing on discrete, marginal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Focusing on discrete marginal issues (e.g., CO2 fertilization) while ignoring the vast majority of impacts misrepresents the scientific literature and understates harms of climate change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a balanced account that situates any highlighted positive or ambiguous effects within the broader evidence of harms across ecosystems, human health, and infrastructure. Avoid selective emphasis that ignores net-negative outcomes (e.g., food security, public health).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use up-to-date, peer-reviewed attribution follow-ups for rapid analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: World Weather Attribution rapid attributions have often later been published in peer-reviewed journals with main findings unchanged; the Draft CWG Report failed to mention this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing rapid attribution studies, note whether follow-up peer-review has confirmed results. Treat rapid attribution as a valid preliminary source but contextualize it with later peer-reviewed work when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground claims about ecosystem resilience in paleoclimate and extinction records
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that corals or other taxa first arose long ago does not mean they are resilient to modern rates/magnitudes of change; fossil records show major extinction events tied to combined ocean changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paleo evidence to evaluate resilience and risks; do not claim long existence implies immunity. Discuss past instances where combined changes in temperature, pH, and oxygen coincided with mass extinctions to inform current risk assessments.
